abstract: Much of biomedical research rests on small, repeated decisions with a fixed set of answers: whether a study belongs in a systematic review, whether two trial claims contradict each other, which type a cell is, whether a peptide-spectrum match is correct. Pretrained decision models answer such questions without training on the data at hand, but how far they can replace the methods established for each task is unknown. Here we tested two such models, Jev and d3-ultra, against an established tool or, where none exists, published benchmark results. We evaluated four tasks with known answers, ordered from text input to numeric input. On text, the models were usable without any training: in screening for 39 systematic reviews, their reading order showed no detectable difference from the active-learning screener ASReview at the ideal stopping point. In detecting contradictory drug-trial claims, they scored close to the best published model. On gene names, they helped only where a curated marker database was weak: they trailed it in pancreas and led it in heart, by a margin that depended strongly on how the database was applied. On numbers from one mass-spectrometry run they accepted 30 to 55% fewer matches at 1% estimated error than a re-scorer trained on that run. Pretrained decision models are therefore a practical first pass for text-based decisions and worth trying where curated knowledge is thin, but no substitute for a tool trained on the experiments own numbers.
